section-87: Classical liberalism developed in the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries as a reaction against absolute monarchy, feudal privilege, religious intolerance and mercantilism. Key thinkers: John Locke (natural rights, limited government, consent), Adam Smith ('The Wealth of Nations', 1776 - the 'invisible hand' of the market and laissez-faire), Jeremy Bentham and James Mill (utilitarianism), Herbert Spencer ('The Man versus the State', 1884) and early J. S. Mill. It was linked with the rise of the bourgeoisie, commerce and industrial capitalism.

It sees the state as a 'necessary evil' and a 'night-watchman' whose functions are limited to defence, law and order, protection of property and enforcement of contracts. Economic freedom - free markets, free trade and private enterprise - is seen as the basis of prosperity and political freedom. Classical liberalism's revival in the late twentieth century is called neo-liberalism (Hayek, 'The Road to Serfdom', 1944; Milton Friedman; Robert Nozick), which influenced the policies of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan and the 'Washington Consensus'.
section-88: Characteristics: (1) individualism - the individual is the centre of society and has rights prior to the state; (2) negative liberty - freedom as absence of restraint; (3) natural rights to life, liberty and property; (4) limited government and constitutionalism - government based on consent, separation of powers and rule of law; (5) laissez-faire economics - minimal state intervention in the economy, free market, free trade and competition; (6) private property as essential to freedom; (7) rationalism - faith in human reason and progress; (8) tolerance, especially religious tolerance; (9) equality before law and equality of opportunity (not of outcome); and (10) a contractual view of society.

Criticisms: socialists and Marxists argued that classical liberalism served the interests of capitalists and ignored the poverty and exploitation of workers; the freedom of the market was 'the freedom of the fox in the hen-house'. The Industrial Revolution's social problems led to the development of positive or welfare liberalism.
section-89: Positive (modern, social or welfare) liberalism developed in late nineteenth-century Britain in response to the problems of industrial capitalism - poverty, unemployment, poor housing, child labour and ill-health. Thinkers include T. H. Green (Oxford idealist, 'Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation', 1882), L. T. Hobhouse ('Liberalism', 1911), J. A. Hobson, John Maynard Keynes ('The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', 1936), William Beveridge (the Beveridge Report, 1942, the basis of the British welfare state), Harold Laski, John Dewey and John Rawls.

Green argued that freedom is 'a positive power or capacity of doing or enjoying something worth doing or enjoying', and that the state should 'hinder hindrances' to the good life, such as ignorance, poverty and disease. Keynes argued for government spending to maintain employment and demand, especially during depressions. Positive liberalism justified the welfare state, social security, public education and health, labour laws and progressive taxation. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal (1930s) and post-war European welfare states reflected it.
section-90: Characteristics: (1) positive liberty - freedom as opportunity and capacity for self-development; (2) the state as a positive good and agent of social welfare, not a necessary evil; (3) welfare state - education, health care, housing, unemployment insurance, pensions and social security; (4) regulation of the economy - labour laws, minimum wages, consumer protection, regulation of monopolies; (5) a mixed economy and Keynesian demand management; (6) social justice and equality of opportunity, including progressive taxation and redistribution; (7) democracy and participation; and (8) retention of individual rights, constitutionalism and private property.

Critics from the right (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick) argue that the welfare state restricts freedom, creates dependency, reduces efficiency and leads to big government ('The Road to Serfdom'). Critics from the left say welfare liberalism does not go far enough to end capitalist inequality. The Indian Constitution's Directive Principles reflect welfare liberal ideas alongside socialist goals.
section-91: Liberal feminism is the oldest and most mainstream form of feminism. Key thinkers and texts: Mary Wollstonecraft ('A Vindication of the Rights of Woman', 1792), arguing that women are rational beings who should receive the same education as men; John Stuart Mill and Harriet Taylor Mill ('The Subjection of Women', 1869), arguing for legal equality and suffrage; Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the Seneca Falls Convention (1848); and Betty Friedan ('The Feminine Mystique', 1963), who founded the National Organization for Women (1966).

Liberal feminism is based on liberal principles of individualism, equal rights, rationality and equality of opportunity. It argues that women's subordination results from legal and customary restrictions that prevent them from entering public life, and that these can be removed through reforms within the existing liberal democratic system - without overthrowing capitalism or the family.
section-92: Core themes: (1) equal rights - women and men are equal as rational individuals and should have equal legal and political rights (suffrage, property, divorce, custody); (2) equal opportunity in education and employment, equal pay for equal work, and anti-discrimination laws; (3) the public-private distinction - liberal feminists focus mainly on the public sphere (law, politics, work), though they also support reproductive rights; (4) reform, not revolution - working through legal and political processes, lobbying and courts; and (5) individual choice and autonomy.

Achievements include women's suffrage, equal pay laws, anti-discrimination laws (Title IX in the USA, 1972), access to higher education and professions, and reproductive rights. Criticisms: radical feminists argue that liberal feminism ignores deeper patriarchal structures in family and sexuality; socialist feminists say it ignores class and capitalism; black and postcolonial feminists say it reflects the concerns of white, middle-class Western women; and it may encourage women to adopt male norms of success. Liberal feminism remains influential in policy-making, including India's legal reforms.
section-93: Radical feminism emerged in the late 1960s and 1970s from the second wave of the women's movement and the New Left in the USA. Key thinkers: Kate Millett ('Sexual Politics', 1970), who defined patriarchy as the most pervasive ideology of our culture; Shulamith Firestone ('The Dialectic of Sex', 1970), who argued that women's oppression is rooted in biology and reproduction and proposed technology (artificial reproduction) to free women; Andrea Dworkin and Catharine MacKinnon (on pornography and sexual violence); Mary Daly ('Gyn/Ecology', 1978); Adrienne Rich; and Germaine Greer ('The Female Eunuch', 1970).

Radical feminists argue that patriarchy - the system of male domination over women - is the oldest, most fundamental and universal form of oppression, existing before class and present in all societies and institutions, especially the family, sexuality and culture. 'Radical' means going to the root of the problem. The slogan 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch, 1969) means that personal relationships - housework, marriage, sex, childbirth - are sites of power and politics.
section-94: Core themes: (1) patriarchy as a system of male domination over women in all spheres; (2) 'the personal is political' - power relations in the family and private life; (3) sexuality and the body - male control of women's bodies through rape, domestic violence, pornography, prostitution, beauty standards and control of reproduction; (4) consciousness-raising - women sharing personal experiences in small groups to recognise common oppression; (5) sisterhood - solidarity among women; (6) separatism - some radical feminists favoured women-only organisations and spaces, and political lesbianism; (7) critique of the family as an institution of oppression; and (8) celebration of women's culture and values (cultural feminism).

Contributions: radical feminism brought issues such as rape, domestic violence, sexual harassment and reproductive freedom into public debate, leading to laws and services (rape crisis centres, shelters for battered women). Criticisms: it is accused of treating all men as oppressors and all women as a single group, ignoring differences of race, class and culture; of biological determinism; and of separatism. Later intersectional and postcolonial feminisms emphasised diversity among women.
section-95: Multiculturalism is both a description of societies with many cultural, ethnic, religious and linguistic groups and a normative theory or policy that seeks recognition and accommodation of such diversity. Canada was the first country to adopt multiculturalism as official policy (1971, under Pierre Trudeau; Canadian Multiculturalism Act, 1988), followed by Australia. Key thinkers include Charles Taylor ('The Politics of Recognition', 1992), Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh ('Rethinking Multiculturalism', 2000), Iris Marion Young ('Justice and the Politics of Difference', 1990) and James Tully.

Multiculturalism challenges the assimilationist model (minorities must adopt the dominant culture - the 'melting pot') and the liberal idea of a 'difference-blind' state. It argues that equal citizenship may require recognising cultural differences and group-specific rights. Critics include conservative nationalists (who fear loss of national identity), liberals such as Brian Barry ('Culture and Equality', 2001), who argue that group rights undermine individual rights and equality, and feminists who note that cultural practices may oppress women (Susan Moller Okin, 'Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?', 1999). Leaders such as Angela Merkel and David Cameron declared in 2010-2011 that multiculturalism had 'failed'. India, with its diverse religions, languages and tribes, is often described as a model of multicultural accommodation.
section-96: Features: (1) recognition of cultural diversity as valuable and legitimate; (2) the politics of recognition (Taylor) - misrecognition or non-recognition of a group's identity can cause harm and inflict a sense of inferiority; (3) group-differentiated rights - special rights for minorities such as self-government, language rights, exemptions from certain laws (for example, Sikhs wearing turbans instead of helmets), and representation; (4) minority protection against assimilation and discrimination; (5) cultural identity as important for individual well-being; (6) intercultural dialogue and mutual respect; and (7) the state should not be culturally neutral in a way that favours the majority culture.

Policy examples: bilingual education, recognition of minority languages, special representation, religious accommodations, affirmative action, autonomy for indigenous peoples and national minorities (Quebec in Canada, Catalonia in Spain, Scotland in the UK). In India, minority educational rights (Article 30), linguistic states, personal laws, the Sixth Schedule and reservations reflect multicultural accommodation.
section-97: Will Kymlicka, a Canadian political philosopher, wrote 'Liberalism, Community and Culture' (1989) and 'Multicultural Citizenship: A Liberal Theory of Minority Rights' (1995). He argues that individual freedom depends on access to a 'societal culture' - a culture that provides meaningful ways of life across public and private spheres, including language, institutions and traditions - which gives individuals the 'context of choice'. Therefore, liberals should protect minority cultures.

He distinguishes two types of minorities: (1) national minorities - previously self-governing, territorially concentrated groups incorporated into a larger state (such as the Québécois, indigenous peoples, Catalans), who are entitled to self-government rights; and (2) polyethnic or immigrant groups, who seek integration with accommodation, entitled to polyethnic rights (such as funding for cultural associations, exemptions from certain laws). A third category is special representation rights. Kymlicka distinguishes 'external protections' (which protect a group from the larger society and are acceptable) from 'internal restrictions' (which limit the freedom of group members and are not acceptable). Critics include Chandran Kukathas (who favours toleration without group rights), Bhikhu Parekh (who says Kymlicka's theory is too liberal and Western) and feminists concerned about women within groups.
section-98: Communitarianism developed in the 1980s as a critique of liberal individualism, especially Rawls's 'A Theory of Justice'. Key thinkers include Alasdair MacIntyre ('After Virtue', 1981), Michael Sandel ('Liberalism and the Limits of Justice', 1982), Charles Taylor ('Sources of the Self', 1989) and Michael Walzer ('Spheres of Justice', 1983). Amitai Etzioni later developed 'responsive communitarianism' as a political movement in the 1990s ('The Spirit of Community', 1993). Its roots go back to Aristotle and Hegel.

Communitarians argue that individuals are shaped by their communities, traditions, families and shared values; that the common good is as important as individual rights; and that liberal theories based on abstract individuals neglect the social foundations of identity and morality. They emphasise civic virtue, social responsibility, participation and community institutions.
section-99: Characteristics: (1) the self is socially embedded or 'situated' - identity is formed through community relationships and traditions; (2) the priority of the common good over individual rights in some cases, or at least balancing rights with responsibilities; (3) importance of shared values, traditions and moral understandings; (4) civic virtue and active citizenship; (5) critique of the 'neutral state' - the state should promote certain conceptions of the good life; (6) importance of intermediate institutions - family, neighbourhood, religious groups, voluntary associations; (7) social responsibility - rights must be accompanied by duties; and (8) concern about the social costs of excessive individualism, such as loneliness, family breakdown, consumerism and declining civic participation (Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone', 2000).

Critics argue that communitarianism can become conservative, majoritarian or oppressive towards minorities and women, since communities may have unjust traditions; that it is vague about which community counts (family, nation, religion?); and that liberals like Rawls (in 'Political Liberalism', 1993) also recognise the importance of community. In India, ideas of community are strong in politics, as in caste and religious identity and Gandhi's vision of village communities.
section-100: Sandel criticised Rawls's idea of an 'unencumbered self' - a person who exists prior to and independent of their ends and attachments, choosing values behind a veil of ignorance. Sandel argues that we are 'encumbered selves', constituted by our attachments to family, community, nation and history; we cannot be understood apart from them. Therefore, Rawls's priority of the right over the good is mistaken.

MacIntyre argued that modern liberal society has lost a shared understanding of virtue and the good life, leading to moral disagreement; he called for a return to Aristotelian virtue ethics rooted in communities and traditions ('narrative unity of life'). Taylor criticised 'atomism' - the view that individuals are self-sufficient - arguing that the capacity for autonomy itself develops only within a society that values it. Walzer argued that principles of justice differ for different goods (money, office, education, healthcare) according to shared social meanings, rejecting a universal theory of justice. These critiques encouraged liberals to take community, identity and civic virtue more seriously.
section-102: Classical liberalism: emerged with the rise of capitalism and the struggle against absolutism and feudalism; thinkers - Locke, Adam Smith, Bentham, Spencer; principles - individualism, natural rights, negative liberty, limited government ('night-watchman state'), laissez-faire, private property, rule of law, free trade and tolerance. It created constitutional government and market economies, but its neglect of social conditions led to poverty and inequality during industrialisation.

Positive liberalism: developed from the late nineteenth century; thinkers - T. H. Green, Hobhouse, Hobson, Keynes, Beveridge, Laski, Rawls; principles - positive liberty, a welfare state, regulation of the economy, social justice, equality of opportunity, public education and health care, and progressive taxation, while retaining individual rights and democracy. It shaped the welfare states of Western Europe, the New Deal and the Indian Directive Principles.

Comparison and later developments: both value individual liberty, but classical liberalism sees the state as a threat to freedom, while positive liberalism sees it as an instrument for creating freedom. From the 1970s, neo-liberalism (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick) revived classical ideas, leading to privatisation, deregulation and globalisation (India's 1991 reforms were influenced by this trend). Contemporary liberals debate the balance between markets and welfare, and Rawls's 'justice as fairness' remains the leading theory of modern liberalism.
section-103: Liberal feminism: based on liberal principles of reason, individual rights and equal opportunity; thinkers - Wollstonecraft, J. S. Mill, Harriet Taylor, Betty Friedan; aims - equal legal and political rights (suffrage, property), equal education and employment, equal pay, anti-discrimination laws and reproductive rights; methods - legal and political reform within the existing system. Achievements include suffrage and many equality laws. Criticisms: focuses on the public sphere and the concerns of middle-class women; accepts liberal capitalist structures.

Radical feminism: patriarchy is the root of women's oppression, present in all institutions, especially the family and sexuality; 'the personal is political'; thinkers - Millett, Firestone, Dworkin, MacKinnon, Daly, Greer; issues - rape, domestic violence, pornography, reproduction, beauty standards, compulsory heterosexuality; methods - consciousness-raising, sisterhood, women-only organisations, cultural transformation; some advocate separatism. Achievements include making violence against women a public issue. Criticisms: essentialism, ignoring differences among women, treating men as a homogeneous oppressor group.

Comparison: both oppose gender inequality, but liberal feminism sees it as the result of discriminatory laws and customs that can be reformed, while radical feminism sees it as a deep structural system requiring fundamental transformation of social and personal relations. Other strands - socialist feminism, black feminism, postcolonial feminism and ecofeminism - add analysis of class, race, colonialism and environment. In India, feminist movements combine legal reform (liberal) with struggles against dowry, rape and patriarchal violence (radical influences).
section-104: Multiculturalism: recognises and accommodates cultural diversity; rejects assimilation and 'difference-blind' liberalism; emphasises the politics of recognition (Charles Taylor), group-differentiated rights, minority protection, and intercultural dialogue (Bhikhu Parekh). Adopted as official policy in Canada (1971) and Australia; debated in Europe. In India, multicultural features include linguistic states, minority rights, personal laws, the Sixth Schedule, special provisions for states (Article 371) and the celebration of diverse festivals and languages.

Kymlicka's liberal multiculturalism: cultural membership provides the 'context of choice' necessary for individual autonomy, so liberal states should protect minority cultures. National minorities deserve self-government rights; immigrant groups deserve polyethnic rights; under-represented groups may deserve special representation. 'External protections' are acceptable, but 'internal restrictions' that limit the freedom of group members are not. Thus Kymlicka reconciles group rights with liberal individual freedom.

Criticisms and debates: liberal critics (Brian Barry) argue that group rights violate equality and may entrench conservative traditions; feminists (Okin) worry about women's rights within groups; communitarians and others (Parekh) argue Kymlicka's framework is too tied to liberal values; and nationalists fear threats to social cohesion. Supporters reply that multiculturalism promotes equal citizenship, inclusion and peace in diverse societies.
section-105: Communitarian critique: Sandel (the 'unencumbered self' versus the 'encumbered' or situated self), MacIntyre (loss of shared virtue and tradition), Taylor (critique of atomism and the social sources of identity), and Walzer (spheres of justice and shared meanings) criticised Rawlsian liberalism for abstract individualism, the priority of rights over the good, and the claim of neutrality. They argued that individuals are constituted by communities, that the common good and civic virtue are essential, and that justice depends on community values.

Communitarian values: social responsibility, duties as well as rights, civic participation, family and community institutions, shared moral traditions and a politics of the common good. Etzioni's responsive communitarianism tried to balance individual rights with social responsibilities and influenced policies such as community service and character education.

Liberal response and evaluation: Rawls's later work ('Political Liberalism', 1993) acknowledged that his theory was political, not metaphysical, and that citizens hold different 'comprehensive doctrines'. Liberals argue that communitarianism risks majoritarianism and oppression of dissenters, minorities and women. The debate has enriched political theory by drawing attention to identity, community and the social conditions of freedom. Communitarianism does not reject liberty but asks that political theory take community seriously.
section-108: Political parties are organised groups of people with similar political views who seek to gain power through elections, form governments and implement their policies. Edmund Burke defined a party as 'a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed'. Joseph Schumpeter described a party as a group whose members act in concert in the competitive struggle for political power. Components of a party: leaders, active members and followers (supporters).

Functions: contesting elections and nominating candidates; forming governments or acting as opposition; formulating policies and programmes (manifestos); aggregating and articulating interests; recruiting and training political leaders; mobilising and educating public opinion; linking citizens with government; and providing stability to democratic systems. Without parties, representative democracy cannot function in large societies.
section-109: Classifications: (1) by geographical reach - national, state or regional parties; (2) by ideology - left (communist and socialist parties - CPI, CPI(M)), centre (the Indian National Congress) and right (conservative, nationalist parties - BJP); (3) by organisation - cadre parties (small, disciplined, ideologically committed, such as communist parties) and mass parties (large membership, broad appeal); Maurice Duverger made this distinction; (4) by social base - class-based, caste-based (BSP), religious (Shiromani Akali Dal, AIMIM), ethnic or regional identity parties (DMK, AIADMK, Shiv Sena, TMC, MNF); and (5) by role - ruling parties, opposition parties; catch-all parties (Otto Kirchheimer) that seek votes from all groups.

Party systems: one-party (China - Communist Party), dominant-party (Congress in India 1952-1967, the LDP in Japan, the ANC in South Africa), two-party (USA - Democrats and Republicans; UK historically - Conservative and Labour) and multi-party (India, France, Germany, Italy).
section-110: Features of the Indian party system: (1) multi-party system with a large number of registered parties (over 2,700 registered parties, of which six are national and around 60 are state parties as of 2024); (2) one-party dominance in the early decades (the 'Congress system', 1952-1967) and again a dominant party since 2014 (BJP); (3) rise of regional parties based on language, region, caste and ethnicity (DMK, TDP, TMC, BJD, SP, BSP, RJD, Shiv Sena, NC, MNF); (4) coalition governments at the Centre from 1989 to 2014 (and dependence on allies since 2024); (5) lack of internal democracy and dynastic politics; (6) personality-centred politics; (7) defections (aaya ram, gaya ram); (8) factionalism; and (9) the role of caste and religion in mobilisation.

Phases (Yogendra Yadav's classification): the Congress system (1952-1967); the Congress-opposition system (1967-1989), with the Janata Party's victory (1977); the third electoral system of coalitions (1989-2014), with the National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA; and BJP dominance since 2014, sometimes called the 'fourth party system'. The party system reflects broader changes in Indian democracy, such as the rise of OBCs, Dalits and regional identities.
section-111: The Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, governs recognition. A party is recognised as a national party if it fulfils any one of the following: (1) it secures at least 6 percent of the valid votes polled in any four or more states in a general election to the Lok Sabha or state assemblies, and in addition wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha; (2) it wins at least 2 percent of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (11 seats) from at least three different states; or (3) it is recognised as a state party in four or more states.

Recognition gives benefits: a reserved symbol throughout India, free broadcast time on public radio and television, consultation in setting election dates and electoral rolls, the right to have 40 'star campaigners' (whose travel expenses are not counted in candidates' expenses) and access to electoral rolls. The Election Commission reviews recognition after each general election. In April 2023, the TMC, NCP and CPI lost national party status, and AAP gained it.
section-112: A party is recognised as a state party in a state if it fulfils any one of the following: (1) it secures at least 6 percent of the valid votes in the state in the last general election to the Lok Sabha or the state assembly, and wins at least one Lok Sabha seat or two assembly seats; (2) it wins at least 3 percent of the total seats in the state assembly or three seats, whichever is more; (3) it wins at least one Lok Sabha seat for every 25 seats allotted to the state; or (4) it secures at least 8 percent of the total valid votes in the state in the last Lok Sabha or assembly election (introduced in 2011, even without winning seats).

A recognised state party gets a reserved symbol in that state and other benefits. In Mizoram, the Mizo National Front (MNF) and the Zoram People's Movement (ZPM) are recognised state parties, and other parties include the Congress and the BJP. State parties play a significant role in Indian federalism and coalition politics.
section-113: Rajni Kothari ('The Congress System in India', 1964) described the 'Congress system' as a one-party dominant system: the Congress won large majorities at the Centre and in most states (1952, 1957 and 1962 elections), but it was a broad, inclusive coalition of diverse interests, groups and factions (a 'party of consensus'), while opposition parties acted as 'parties of pressure' that influenced the Congress from outside. W. H. Morris-Jones described it as a 'dominance-coexistence' system. The Congress dominance was based on its role in the freedom struggle, Nehru's leadership, its organisation and its ability to accommodate different groups.

This dominance was challenged in 1967, when non-Congress governments came to power in several states, and broken in 1977 by the Janata Party. Since 2014, the BJP's victories (with majorities in 2014 and 2019) have led some scholars (Suhas Palshikar, Yogendra Yadav) to describe a new 'BJP system' of one-party dominance, though the BJP fell short of a majority in 2024 and relies on NDA allies. Similar dominant-party systems include the LDP in Japan, the ANC in South Africa and the PRI in Mexico (1929-2000).
section-114: Coalition governments in India: at the Centre - the Janata Party (1977-1979, a merger of parties), the National Front (V. P. Singh, 1989-1990, supported by the BJP and Left), Chandra Shekhar (1990-1991, supported by Congress), the United Front (H. D. Deve Gowda and I. K. Gujral, 1996-1998), the National Democratic Alliance (Atal Bihari Vajpayee, 1998-2004), the United Progressive Alliance (Manmohan Singh, 2004-2014) and the NDA under Narendra Modi (since 2014, with the BJP's own majority in 2014 and 2019, and dependence on allies such as the TDP and JD(U) since 2024). Coalitions have also been common in states, beginning with the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments of 1967.

Features: a Common Minimum Programme; coordination committees; 'coalition dharma'; bargaining over portfolios; and the influence of regional parties. Effects: increased federal balance and representation of regional and social groups; consensus-based policy-making; but also instability (the fall of the Vajpayee government by one vote in 1999), policy paralysis and pressure from allies. Scholars such as E. Sridharan argue that coalitions became the 'new normal' in India's diverse party system.
section-115: The Communist Party of India was formed in 1920 at Tashkent (USSR) by M. N. Roy and others; communist groups held a conference in Kanpur in 1925, regarded by the CPI as its founding date. During the freedom struggle, communists organised trade unions (AITUC) and peasant movements (All India Kisan Sabha), but were banned at times and opposed the Quit India movement in 1942. After independence, the CPI led the Telangana armed struggle (1946-1951) and then took part in parliamentary elections, becoming the main opposition party in the first Lok Sabha (1952). In 1957, it formed the first elected communist government in the world in Kerala under E. M. S. Namboodiripad (dismissed in 1959 under Article 356).

In 1964, the party split: the CPI(M) was formed by those who criticised the CPI's closeness to the Congress and the Soviet line. Later, the CPI(ML) (Naxalites, 1969) split from the CPI(M). The CPI supported Indira Gandhi's Emergency (1975-1977). Its ideology is Marxism-Leninism, with goals of socialism, land reforms, workers' rights and secularism. Its influence has declined; it lost national party status in 2023. The Left parties have been strong in Kerala, West Bengal (Left Front government 1977-2011) and Tripura (until 2018).
section-116: The BJP was founded on 6 April 1980 by leaders of the former Bharatiya Jana Sangh (founded in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mookerjee), which had merged into the Janata Party in 1977. Atal Bihari Vajpayee was its first president. Its ideological roots lie in the RSS and Hindutva (cultural nationalism), with principles of 'integral humanism' (Deendayal Upadhyaya, 1965), Gandhian socialism (in its early years), a strong nation, cultural nationalism, and opposition to 'minority appeasement'. Key issues have included the Ram Janmabhoomi movement (L. K. Advani's Rath Yatra, 1990), the abrogation of Article 370 (achieved in 2019), the Uniform Civil Code and the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019).

Electoral growth: from 2 Lok Sabha seats in 1984 to 85 in 1989, 120 in 1991, 161 in 1996 (Vajpayee's 13-day government), 182 in 1998 and 1999 (NDA government), 282 in 2014 and 303 in 2019 under Narendra Modi (the first single-party majority since 1984), and 240 in 2024, forming the government with NDA allies. It governs many states and claims to be the world's largest political party by membership. Its supporters credit it with strong leadership, development and national security; critics raise concerns about majoritarianism, minority rights and centralisation.
section-117: The ECI (Article 324) is a permanent constitutional body, established on 25 January 1950, consisting of the Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners (since 1993). It superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. Its functions include preparing electoral rolls, issuing voter IDs, recognising parties and allotting symbols, announcing election schedules, enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, monitoring expenditure, appointing observers, conducting polls using EVMs and VVPAT, and advising on disqualifications.

The ECI's independence and impartiality are essential for free and fair elections. T. N. Seshan's tenure (1990-1996) made it a powerful institution. Recent issues include the appointment process (the 2023 Act), allegations of bias in enforcing the Model Code, debates about EVMs and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls (Bihar, 2025), which raised concerns about deletion of voters. Public trust in the ECI is vital for Indian democracy.
section-118: The Representation of the People Act, 1950, deals with allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies (with the Delimitation Act), qualifications of voters and preparation of electoral rolls. The Representation of the People Act, 1951, deals with the actual conduct of elections: qualifications and disqualifications of members (Sections 8-11, including disqualification on conviction for certain offences - the Supreme Court in Lily Thomas v. Union of India, 2013, ruled that convicted legislators are disqualified immediately); notification of elections; nominations, scrutiny and withdrawal; election agents; election expenses (limits set by rules, currently up to 95 lakh rupees for Lok Sabha candidates in larger states); conduct of polls and counting; registration of political parties (Section 29A); election disputes through election petitions filed in High Courts (Section 80); and corrupt practices (bribery, undue influence, appeal on grounds of religion, caste or community - Section 123) and electoral offences.

Amendments have introduced disclosure of contributions to parties (Section 29C), the use of EVMs, voting rights for overseas Indians (2010, in person), postal ballots for certain categories, the Model Code-related provisions and the ban on exit polls during specified periods. The Act is the main legal framework for India's electoral process.
section-119: Frequent defections in the 1960s and 1970s ('Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram' - named after Haryana MLA Gaya Lal, who changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967) destabilised governments. The 52nd Amendment Act (1985), under Rajiv Gandhi, added the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. A member of a House is disqualified if he or she voluntarily gives up membership of the party, or votes or abstains contrary to the party's whip without permission (unless condoned within 15 days). An independent member is disqualified if he or she joins a party, and a nominated member if he or she joins a party after six months.

The original law exempted a 'split' if one-third of a legislature party left; the 91st Amendment (2003) removed this exemption, so only a merger supported by two-thirds of the legislature party is protected. The Speaker or Chairman decides on disqualification; in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the law but made the Speaker's decisions subject to judicial review. Criticisms: the law curbs the freedom of legislators to express dissent, gives too much power to party leaders, and the Speaker's decisions are often delayed or partisan (the Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020, suggested an independent tribunal). Defections through mass resignations and mergers continue.
section-120: Reforms implemented: lowering the voting age to 18 (61st Amendment, 1988); EVMs (nationwide since 2004) and VVPAT; Electors' Photo Identity Cards (1993); the anti-defection law (1985, 2003); disclosure of criminal records, assets and educational qualifications of candidates (Supreme Court in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms, 2002, and PUCL, 2003); NOTA (2013); limits on election expenditure; the Model Code of Conduct; ban on exit polls during voting; immediate disqualification of convicted legislators (Lily Thomas, 2013); and the requirement for parties to publish criminal records of candidates and reasons for selecting them (2020).

Committees on electoral reform include the Tarkunde Committee (1974), Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Indrajit Gupta Committee on state funding (1998), Law Commission reports (170th, 1999; 255th, 2015) and the Election Commission's proposals. Pending issues include state funding of elections, transparency in political donations (the electoral bond scheme, 2018, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024 as violating the right to information), decriminalisation, inner-party democracy, regulation of social media and paid news, simultaneous elections ('One Nation, One Election' - the Kovind Committee report, 2024, and the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill introduced in 2024), and remote voting for migrant workers.
section-121: Bipan Chandra ('Communalism in Modern India', 1984) defined communalism as the belief that because a group of people follow a particular religion, they have common social, political and economic interests, which are different from and opposed to the interests of followers of other religions. He identified three stages: (1) communal nationalism - followers of a religion have common secular interests; (2) liberal communalism - interests of different religious communities are different; and (3) extreme communalism - interests of different religions are mutually incompatible and hostile, leading to hatred and violence.

Communalism should be distinguished from religiosity: being religious is not communal; communalism is the political use of religion. Forms include political mobilisation on religious lines, communal riots, hate speech, discrimination against minorities, and demands for separate states on religious grounds (as in the Partition of 1947). Major incidents in India: Partition violence (1947), the anti-Sikh riots (1984), the demolition of the Babri Masjid (1992) and subsequent riots, the Gujarat riots (2002), Muzaffarnagar (2013) and Delhi (2020).
section-122: Historical causes: British 'divide and rule' policies (separate electorates in 1909, communal representation and the Communal Award of 1932), communal interpretations of history (portraying the medieval period as Muslim tyranny and the ancient period as a Hindu golden age), and the trauma of Partition. Political causes: vote-bank politics, mobilisation of religious identity by parties and leaders for electoral gain, and the role of communal organisations.

Social and economic causes: economic backwardness, unemployment and competition for jobs and resources; lack of education; segregation of communities in housing; prejudices and stereotypes; and fears of minorities about their identity and security. Other factors: the role of media and social media in spreading rumours and hate speech; the failure of the administration and police to act impartially; external factors (cross-border terrorism, international events); and religious fundamentalism. Communalism is a modern phenomenon linked with politics rather than an inevitable result of religious differences.
section-123: Remedies: (1) strict enforcement of the rule of law and punishment of those who incite or commit communal violence; impartial police and administration; quick justice for victims (the Communal Violence Bill was proposed in 2011 but not passed); (2) secular education and textbooks that promote tolerance, scientific temper and a balanced view of history; (3) responsible political leadership - banning appeals to religion in elections (Section 123(3) of the RPA, 1951; the Supreme Court in Abhiram Singh, 2017, held that appeals to religion, caste or community of the voter or candidate are corrupt practices); (4) economic development and reduction of inequality and unemployment; (5) inter-community dialogue, peace committees and civil society initiatives; (6) responsible media and regulation of hate speech and fake news; (7) protection of minority rights and equal citizenship; and (8) promotion of composite culture and shared festivals.

Institutions such as the National Integration Council (1961), the National Commission for Minorities (1992) and peace committees in districts help in prevention. In Mizoram and other Northeast states, civil society bodies such as churches and youth organisations play a role in maintaining social harmony, though ethnic tensions also need careful management.
section-124: Regionalism refers to a feeling of loyalty to a particular region based on language, culture, ethnicity, history, geography or economic interests, and the political mobilisation that results from it. It can be positive (a sense of regional identity, pride and demands for development and autonomy within the nation) or negative (when it becomes parochial, hostile to others or secessionist).

Causes in India: linguistic and cultural diversity; uneven economic development and regional disparities (for example, between developed states like Maharashtra and Gujarat and backward regions like parts of Bihar and the Northeast); historical factors (princely states, colonial administration); geographical isolation (the Northeast); neglect by the central government; 'sons of the soil' movements over jobs and migration (Shiv Sena in Maharashtra, Assam Movement); the role of regional parties and leaders; and ethnic identity. The Constitution accommodates regionalism through federalism, linguistic states, the Sixth Schedule, Article 371 provisions and the Finance Commission.
section-125: Forms: (1) demands for separate statehood within India - the formation of Andhra (1953) after Potti Sriramulu's fast-unto-death, linguistic reorganisation (1956), Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), Punjab and Haryana (1966), Northeast states (1963-1987), Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand (2000), Telangana (2014), and continuing demands (Gorkhaland, Vidarbha, Bodoland); (2) demands for greater autonomy (the DMK in Tamil Nadu, the Anandpur Sahib Resolution in Punjab, 1973, and state autonomy demands in Jammu and Kashmir); (3) inter-state disputes over boundaries (Belgaum between Karnataka and Maharashtra, Assam with its neighbours including Mizoram) and river waters (Kaveri, Krishna, Mahadayi, Ravi-Beas); (4) 'sons of the soil' movements against migrants; (5) secessionist movements (Khalistan in Punjab in the 1980s, insurgencies in the Northeast, militancy in Kashmir); and (6) regional political parties representing regional interests.

Regionalism has strengthened Indian federalism and given voice to regional identities, but its extreme forms threaten national integration. Balanced regional development, decentralisation, cultural recognition and dialogue are seen as solutions.
section-126: Constitutional provisions: Article 15(4) - special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs; Article 15(5) - reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided ones (93rd Amendment, 2005); Article 16(4) - reservation in public appointments; Article 16(4A) - reservation in promotions (77th Amendment, 1995); Article 16(4B) - carry forward of unfilled vacancies (81st Amendment, 2000); Article 46 - promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs and STs; Article 330 and 332 - reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies (84 SC and 47 ST seats in the Lok Sabha); Article 334 - the time limit for legislative reservations (extended every ten years, now until 2030 by the 104th Amendment); Article 335 - claims of SCs and STs in services consistent with efficiency; Article 338 and 338A - National Commissions for SCs and STs; Article 243D and 243T - reservations in panchayats and municipalities; and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas.

In central government jobs, the reservation is 15 percent for SCs and 7.5 percent for STs (in addition to 27 percent for OBCs and 10 percent for EWS). In Mizoram, most Assembly seats (39 of 40) are reserved for STs because of the predominantly tribal population. Debates include the 50 percent cap (Indra Sawhney, 1992), sub-classification within SCs (allowed by the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, 2024), the creamy layer, and reservation in the private sector.
section-128: Nature of the party system: India has a multi-party system with national parties (BJP, INC, CPI(M), BSP, AAP, NPP), recognised state parties and thousands of registered unrecognised parties. Recognition is governed by the Election Symbols Order, 1968, based on vote share and seats. Parties can be classified by ideology (left, centre, right), social base (caste, religion, region, class) and organisation (cadre and mass parties).

Evolution: (1) one-party dominance of the Congress (1952-1967), described by Rajni Kothari as the 'Congress system'; (2) the decline of Congress dominance and rise of opposition (1967-1989), including the Janata Party government (1977-1980); (3) fragmentation, regionalisation and coalition governments (1989-2014), with the rise of the BJP, regional parties and parties representing OBCs and Dalits after the Mandal Commission; and (4) the re-emergence of a dominant party (BJP) since 2014, though dependent on allies since 2024. Regional parties have remained powerful in many states, such as Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Punjab.

Problems and reforms: lack of internal democracy, dynastic politics, personality cults, defections, criminalisation, opaque funding and the use of money and muscle power. Reforms suggested include regulation of internal party elections, transparency of funds, state funding, strengthening the anti-defection law and decriminalisation. The party system is an indicator of the deepening of democracy and the representation of new social groups.
section-129: Single-party dominance: the Congress system (Kothari) - a broad consensus party, accommodating diverse groups and factions, with opposition parties influencing it from outside; based on the legacy of the freedom movement, Nehru's leadership and organisational strength; broken in 1967 and 1977. The BJP's dominance since 2014 is based on strong leadership, Hindutva and nationalism, welfare schemes, organisational strength (RSS network) and a weak opposition, though it lost its majority in 2024.

Coalition politics (1989-2014): governments of the National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA; features - Common Minimum Programmes, coordination committees, bargaining and the influence of regional parties; effects - greater federalism and representation, but also instability and policy compromises. Coalitions are also common at the state level and in post-poll alliances.

Left and right parties: the CPI (founded 1925, Marxist-Leninist, led trade unions and peasant movements, formed the first elected communist government in Kerala, 1957, split in 1964 into CPI and CPI(M), declining today) represents the left; the BJP (founded 1980 from the Jana Sangh, rooted in Hindutva and integral humanism, rose from 2 seats in 1984 to dominance after 2014) represents the right. The Congress occupies the centre. The changing balance of left, centre and right reflects shifts in Indian society and politics, from Nehruvian socialism to economic liberalisation and cultural nationalism.
section-130: Election Commission: constitutional body under Article 324; three members; functions - electoral rolls, recognition of parties and symbols, conduct of elections, Model Code of Conduct, expenditure monitoring, EVMs and VVPAT; reforms under T. N. Seshan; challenges - money power, criminalisation, misinformation, questions of independence. Representation of the People Act, 1951: governs qualifications and disqualifications, nominations, election expenses, conduct of polls, registration of parties, corrupt practices (including appeals on grounds of religion, caste and community) and election disputes.

Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule): introduced by the 52nd Amendment (1985) and strengthened by the 91st Amendment (2003); disqualifies members who voluntarily give up party membership or defy the whip; exemption for mergers of two-thirds; the Speaker decides, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992). Criticisms: restricts dissent, gives Speakers partisan discretion, delays decisions, and has not prevented defections through resignations and mergers.

Electoral reforms: implemented - voting age 18, EVMs and VVPAT, voter IDs, disclosure of criminal records and assets, NOTA, immediate disqualification on conviction, expenditure limits; proposed - state funding, transparency in donations (after the electoral bonds judgement, 2024), decriminalisation, inner-party democracy, regulation of social media, simultaneous elections and remote voting. Together, these institutions and laws form the framework for free and fair elections in India.
section-131: Communalism: the belief that religious communities have separate and opposed interests; stages (Bipan Chandra) - communal nationalism, liberal communalism and extreme communalism; causes - colonial divide and rule, communal history, Partition, vote-bank politics, economic competition, prejudice, media and fundamentalism; manifestations - riots, hate speech, discrimination, polarisation. Remedies - rule of law and impartial administration, secular education, responsible leadership and legal bans on religious appeals in elections, economic development, inter-community dialogue, responsible media and protection of minority rights. Secularism (S. R. Bommai, 1994) is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Regionalism: loyalty to a region based on language, culture, ethnicity or economic interest; causes - diversity, uneven development, neglect, historical and geographical factors, regional parties and migration; forms - statehood demands, autonomy demands, inter-state disputes, sons-of-the-soil movements and secessionism. The States Reorganisation Commission (1953-1955), linguistic states (1956), new states (1960-2014) and special provisions (Articles 371A-J, Sixth Schedule) show how the Constitution accommodates regional aspirations.

Conclusion: both communalism and regionalism arise from India's diversity. Democratic and federal institutions can accommodate diversity, but when identity politics becomes exclusive and hostile, it threatens national unity and democracy. Managing diversity requires constitutional values, inclusive development, decentralisation, tolerance and responsible political leadership.
section-132: Rationale: SCs (formerly 'untouchables', about 16.6 percent of the population in 2011) and STs (tribal communities, about 8.6 percent) suffered historical injustice - untouchability, exclusion from education and property, and geographical isolation. Formal equality would perpetuate their disadvantage, so the Constitution provides 'protective discrimination' to achieve substantive equality and representation, as part of social justice (Preamble, Articles 38, 46). Ambedkar and the Constituent Assembly considered reservations essential.

Provisions: reservation in legislatures (Articles 330, 332, extended until 2030), in local bodies (Articles 243D, 243T), in public employment (Articles 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B), 335) and in educational institutions (Articles 15(4), 15(5)); the National Commissions for SCs (Article 338) and STs (Article 338A, created by the 89th Amendment, 2003); the abolition of untouchability (Article 17); the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) and Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of the Northeast); and laws such as the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989), the PESA Act (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).

Debates and evaluation: reservations have increased representation of SCs and STs in legislatures, government services and education, and created a new middle class among them. Criticisms include the benefits going mainly to the better-off sections (creamy layer debate - the Supreme Court in 2024 suggested a creamy layer for SCs and STs too), inadequate implementation (unfilled posts), reservations in promotions, the 50 percent ceiling, and the argument for economic criteria. Supporters argue that caste discrimination persists and reservations remain necessary. Reservation connects democratic representation with the constitutional goal of addressing entrenched inequality.
section-135: Woodrow Wilson's essay 'The Study of Administration' (1887) is considered the starting point of the discipline; he is called the father of Public Administration. He proposed the politics-administration dichotomy - politics sets goals, and administration implements them efficiently. Definitions: Wilson - 'detailed and systematic execution of public law'; L. D. White - 'all those operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'; Luther Gulick - 'that part of the science of administration which has to do with government'; Dwight Waldo - 'the art and science of management as applied to the affairs of state'.

Public administration differs from private (business) administration in its aims (public interest versus profit), accountability (to legislatures, courts and citizens), legal framework, scale, monopoly of services and political environment, though both share techniques of management. Paul Appleby emphasised that public administration is different because of its political character and public accountability.
section-136: Narrow and broad views: the narrow (managerial) view considers only executive activities (Gulick, Simon), while the broad (integral) view includes all activities of government - legislative, executive and judicial (L. D. White, Marshall Dimock). Luther Gulick's POSDCORB describes the managerial functions of the chief executive: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting. Critics say POSDCORB ignores the substantive content of administration (the subject matter of departments like health, education and defence).

Modern scope includes organisation theory, personnel administration, financial administration, public policy, comparative and development administration, local government, administrative law and accountability, e-governance, public-private partnerships and governance. Approaches have evolved from classical theory to New Public Administration (Minnowbrook Conference, 1968, emphasising relevance, values, equity and change), New Public Management (1980s-1990s, emphasising market principles, efficiency, results and 'reinventing government' - Osborne and Gaebler, 1992), New Public Service (Denhardt) and good governance.
section-137: Significance: public administration is the 'heart of the modern state' (Brooks Adams said it is 'the capacity of coordinating many, and often conflicting, social energies in a single organism'). It implements laws and policies, delivers essential services (education, health, water, transport), maintains law and order, collects revenue, manages emergencies (disasters, pandemics), promotes economic development and social welfare, protects the environment, and provides continuity and stability even when governments change.

In developing countries like India, administration plays a key role in nation-building and development (rural development, poverty alleviation, welfare schemes such as MGNREGA and the Public Distribution System). The quality of administration determines whether policies succeed. Challenges include corruption, red tape, inefficiency, lack of accountability and politicisation; reforms aim at good governance, transparency (RTI), citizen charters, e-governance (Digital India, direct benefit transfers) and decentralisation.
section-138: Frederick Winslow Taylor (1856-1915), an American engineer, is the father of scientific management ('The Principles of Scientific Management', 1911). Based on time-and-motion studies at Midvale Steel and Bethlehem Steel, he argued that there is 'one best way' to do any job, which can be discovered scientifically. Principles: (1) scientific study of each element of work to replace rule-of-thumb methods; (2) scientific selection, training and development of workers; (3) cooperation between management and workers to ensure work is done according to scientific principles; and (4) division of responsibility between management (planning) and workers (execution). He also proposed functional foremanship (eight specialised foremen instead of one) and differential piece-rate wages to motivate workers.

Others in the classical tradition include Henri Fayol (14 principles of management, such as division of work, unity of command, scalar chain and esprit de corps), Luther Gulick and Lyndall Urwick (POSDCORB), Frank and Lillian Gilbreth (motion studies) and Henry Gantt (Gantt charts). Criticisms: treats workers as machines ('economic man') motivated only by money; ignores human and social factors; leads to monotony and exploitation; and was opposed by trade unions. Nevertheless, it improved productivity and laid the foundations of management science.
section-139: The human relations approach arose from the Hawthorne experiments (1924-1932) at the Western Electric Company's Hawthorne Works near Chicago, led by Elton Mayo, F. J. Roethlisberger and W. J. Dickson of Harvard. The experiments included illumination studies (productivity increased whether lighting was increased or decreased), relay assembly test room studies (productivity increased due to attention and group cohesion - the 'Hawthorne effect'), interviews, and the bank wiring room study (informal groups set their own production norms).

Findings: workers are social beings with emotional needs, not just economic beings; informal groups, social relationships, morale, communication, participation and supervision style strongly influence productivity; non-economic rewards (recognition, belonging) matter; and the organisation is a social system. Later behavioural theorists - Abraham Maslow (hierarchy of needs), Douglas McGregor (Theory X and Theory Y), Frederick Herzberg (two-factor theory), Chris Argyris and Rensis Likert - developed these insights. Criticisms: overemphasis on human relations and informal groups, neglect of formal structure and economic factors, and potential manipulation of workers by management.
section-140: Max Weber (1864-1920), a German sociologist, developed the 'ideal type' of bureaucracy based on legal-rational authority ('Economy and Society', published 1922). Characteristics: (1) hierarchy of offices with a clear chain of command; (2) a division of labour and specialisation; (3) a system of rules and regulations governing official decisions; (4) impersonality - decisions based on rules, not personal feelings; (5) written documents and records (files); (6) officials appointed on merit through examinations and qualifications; (7) full-time, salaried career officials with tenure, pensions and promotions based on seniority or merit; and (8) separation of the official from ownership of the means of administration.

Weber considered bureaucracy the most efficient form of organisation for large-scale tasks, but feared that it could become an 'iron cage' that limits freedom. Criticisms: Robert Merton (bureaucratic dysfunctions - 'trained incapacity', goal displacement, rigidity, red tape), Philip Selznick, Alvin Gouldner, Michel Crozier and others pointed to inefficiency, resistance to change, delays and lack of responsiveness. Marxists see bureaucracy as serving the ruling class. Nonetheless, bureaucracy remains the basic structure of modern government, including the Indian civil services.
section-141: Organisation is both a structure (the pattern of relationships among positions) and a process (organising activities). L. D. White defined organisation as 'the arrangement of personnel for facilitating the accomplishment of some agreed purpose through the allocation of functions and responsibilities'. Chester Barnard ('The Functions of the Executive', 1938) defined it as 'a system of consciously coordinated activities or forces of two or more persons', requiring communication, willingness to serve and a common purpose.

Types: formal organisation (planned structure, rules, official roles, organisational charts) and informal organisation (social relationships, groups and norms that develop naturally). Principles of organisation include hierarchy (scalar chain), unity of command (one superior for each subordinate), span of control (the number of subordinates one supervisor can manage effectively - Graicunas's formula), delegation, coordination, centralisation and decentralisation, and line and staff agencies. Forms of public organisations include departments, ministries, public corporations (such as the Life Insurance Corporation), independent regulatory commissions, boards and commissions.
section-142: Hierarchy (scalar principle) means the arrangement of positions in a graded order, like a pyramid, with authority flowing from the top to the bottom and responsibility and communication flowing upward. Henri Fayol described the 'scalar chain' and the 'gangplank' - allowing direct horizontal communication between officials at the same level, with superiors' permission, to avoid delays. In Indian administration, a typical hierarchy is Secretary - Additional Secretary - Joint Secretary - Director - Deputy Secretary - Under Secretary - Section Officer - Assistants.

Merits: clear lines of authority and responsibility, unity of command, coordination, delegation, discipline and channels of communication. Demerits: rigidity, delays and red tape, distortion of communication as it passes through many levels, concentration of power at the top, and discouragement of initiative and creativity at lower levels. Modern organisations use flatter structures, teams and networks to overcome these problems.
section-143: Centralisation means the concentration of decision-making authority at the top of an organisation or at the central government. Advantages: uniformity of policies and standards, strong leadership and control, coordination, efficient use of specialised resources, quick decisions in emergencies and national unity. Disadvantages: overload and delays at the top, distance from local conditions and needs, lack of initiative at lower levels, reduced participation and responsiveness, and the risk of authoritarianism.

Factors favouring centralisation include small organisations, national emergencies, the need for uniformity, a lack of competent lower-level personnel and modern communication technology. In India, the Union government's strong powers, central schemes and All-India Services reflect centralising tendencies, while demands for state autonomy and local government reflect pressures for decentralisation.
section-144: Decentralisation means the transfer of authority and responsibility from the central level to lower levels or local units. Forms: (1) deconcentration (administrative decentralisation) - transfer of work to field offices of the central government; (2) delegation - transfer of specific powers to semi-autonomous bodies; (3) devolution (political decentralisation) - transfer of powers to elected local governments with their own authority and resources; and (4) privatisation or divestment - transfer of functions to private or non-governmental organisations. Decentralisation may be functional (by subject) or territorial (by area).

Advantages: faster decisions, responsiveness to local needs, people's participation and democracy at the grassroots, reduced burden on the centre, development of local leadership and accountability. Disadvantages: lack of uniformity, coordination problems, inadequate resources and capacity at lower levels, and capture by local elites. In India, the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) created a three-tier system of panchayats and municipalities with 29 subjects (Eleventh Schedule) and 18 subjects (Twelfth Schedule), and reserved one-third of seats for women. Mizoram has Village Councils and Autonomous District Councils instead of panchayats.
section-145: Leadership is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards organisational goals. Theories: (1) trait theory - leaders have innate qualities such as intelligence, confidence, integrity, initiative and decisiveness ('great man' theory); (2) behavioural theories - focus on what leaders do; the Ohio State and Michigan studies identified task-oriented and people-oriented behaviour; Kurt Lewin's styles - autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire; Blake and Mouton's managerial grid; (3) contingency or situational theories - effective leadership depends on the situation (Fred Fiedler's contingency model; Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership; House's path-goal theory); and (4) transformational leadership (James MacGregor Burns, Bernard Bass), which inspires followers to go beyond self-interest for a shared vision, versus transactional leadership, based on rewards and punishments.

Functions of administrative leadership: setting goals, planning, organising, motivating, communicating, coordinating, making decisions, representing the organisation and building morale. Chester Barnard emphasised the leader's role in communication and creating cooperation. Good leadership is essential for effective public administration.
section-146: Herbert Simon ('Administrative Behaviour', 1947; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1978) argued that decision-making is the heart of administration. He criticised classical 'principles' of administration as 'proverbs' that contradict each other. Steps in rational decision-making: (1) intelligence activity - identifying the problem; (2) design activity - developing alternatives; and (3) choice activity - selecting the best alternative; followed by implementation and review.

Simon introduced 'bounded rationality': because of limited information, time and cognitive ability, administrators cannot find the optimal solution, so they 'satisfice' - choose a satisfactory and sufficient alternative ('administrative man' versus 'economic man'). Charles Lindblom's 'science of muddling through' (1959) described incrementalism - making small, gradual changes from existing policies. Amitai Etzioni proposed 'mixed scanning', combining rational and incremental approaches. Other models include the garbage can model (Cohen, March and Olsen) and group decision-making. Decisions may be programmed (routine) or non-programmed (new and complex).
section-147: Accountability means that public officials and agencies must answer for their actions, decisions and use of public resources to the people, legislature, courts and higher authorities, and face consequences for misconduct. Types: (1) legislative control - questions, debates, committees (Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings), budget approval, no-confidence motions; (2) executive control - ministers, cabinet, civil service rules, budget and audit, appointment and removal; (3) judicial control - judicial review, writs, PIL, administrative tribunals; and (4) popular control - elections, public opinion, media, civil society, citizen charters, social audits, the Right to Information Act (2005), and grievance redressal mechanisms (Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, CPGRAMS).

Other institutions: the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Central Vigilance Commission (1964, statutory since 2003), the Lokpal (Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; first Lokpal appointed in 2019) and Lokayuktas in states, the Central Bureau of Investigation, and the Ombudsman idea (from Sweden, 1809). Accountability helps prevent corruption, abuse of power and inefficiency.
section-148: Recruitment means attracting and selecting suitable candidates for public service. Types: direct recruitment (from outside, through competitive examinations) and indirect recruitment (by promotion from within). In India, recruitment is done by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC, Article 315-323, originally the Public Service Commission of 1926) for All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and central services; State Public Service Commissions (including the Mizoram Public Service Commission) for state services; and the Staff Selection Commission for lower-level posts. The merit-based system was introduced by the Charter Act of 1853 and the Macaulay Committee (1854), based on open competitive examinations.

Methods include written examinations, interviews (personality tests), aptitude tests, group discussions, physical tests and probation. Principles: merit, equal opportunity, transparency and impartiality. Reservations for SCs, STs, OBCs, EWS and persons with disabilities are applied. Lateral entry of specialists at joint secretary and director levels was introduced in 2018, but the 2024 advertisement was withdrawn after criticism about lack of reservation. Issues include delays, coaching-centre culture and the need to test practical skills.
section-149: Training aims to improve knowledge, skills, attitudes and efficiency of public servants, prepare them for higher responsibilities, keep them updated on new technologies and policies and develop values of integrity and service. Types: pre-entry training (education before joining), post-entry training (after joining), orientation or induction training, in-service training, refresher courses, on-the-job training (learning by working under supervision), and formal training in institutions.

Training institutions in India: the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA, Mussoorie) for IAS and other services; the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy (Hyderabad); the Indira Gandhi National Forest Academy (Dehradun); the Indian Institute of Public Administration (New Delhi); and state Administrative Training Institutes (including the Administrative Training Institute in Aizawl). The National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building - 'Mission Karmayogi' (2020) - aims at competency-based, online training through the iGOT platform.
section-150: Promotion means advancement of an employee to a higher post with greater responsibilities, status and pay. It motivates employees, retains talent, rewards experience and merit, and fills higher posts with people familiar with the organisation. Principles: (1) seniority - promotion based on length of service, which is objective and avoids favouritism but may not reward efficiency; (2) merit - based on performance, ability and achievements, assessed through annual performance appraisal reports (APARs), examinations or interviews, which encourages efficiency but may involve subjectivity; and (3) seniority-cum-merit or merit-cum-seniority, combining both.

In India, promotions are decided by Departmental Promotion Committees (DPCs). Reservations in promotion for SCs and STs are allowed under Article 16(4A), subject to conditions laid down by the Supreme Court (M. Nagaraj, 2006 - quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequacy of representation, and efficiency; Jarnail Singh, 2018, removed the requirement of proving backwardness for SCs and STs). Problems include stagnation, delays and litigation.
section-151: The word 'budget' comes from the French 'bougette', meaning a small leather bag. In India, the Constitution uses the term 'Annual Financial Statement' (Article 112). A budget is a statement of estimated revenues and expenditures of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March in India). It is also an instrument of economic policy, planning, accountability and control.

Types: line-item budget (traditional, listing items of expenditure); performance budget (relating expenditure to activities and results, introduced in the USA by the Hoover Commission, 1949, and in India in 1969); planning-programming-budgeting system (PPBS, USA, 1960s); zero-based budgeting (every item justified from zero each year, by Peter Pyhrr; tried in India from 1986); outcome budget (India, 2005, focusing on outcomes); gender budgeting (India, 2005-2006, showing allocations for women); and green budgeting. Budget classification includes revenue and capital budgets, plan and non-plan expenditure (abolished in 2017-2018), and charged and voted expenditure.
section-152: Stages: (1) preparation by the executive - the Ministry of Finance's Budget Division (Department of Economic Affairs) issues a budget circular, ministries submit estimates, the Finance Ministry consults and consolidates, and the Cabinet approves; (2) presentation - the Finance Minister presents the budget in the Lok Sabha (since 2017, on 1 February; the separate Railway Budget was merged into the general budget in 2017); the Economic Survey is presented a day earlier; (3) general discussion in both Houses; (4) scrutiny by Departmentally Related Standing Committees; (5) voting on demands for grants by the Lok Sabha (the Rajya Sabha can only discuss); cut motions (policy cut, economy cut, token cut) may be moved; 'guillotine' applies to remaining demands; (6) passing of the Appropriation Bill (authorising withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund, Article 114) and the Finance Bill (tax proposals, Article 117); and (7) execution and audit.

Other provisions: vote on account (Article 116) allows expenditure for part of the year before the budget is passed, especially in election years; supplementary, additional and excess grants (Article 115); and charged expenditure (such as salaries of the President, judges and the CAG, and debt charges), which is not voted on. Public funds include the Consolidated Fund (Article 266), the Contingency Fund (Article 267) and the Public Account. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (2003) sets targets for fiscal deficit. Parliamentary control through the PAC and the CAG ensures accountability.
section-153: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Articles 148-151) is appointed by the President for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and can be removed only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge. Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution. The CAG's salary and expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund; after leaving office, the CAG is not eligible for further government office. The CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.

Functions (CAG's Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service Act, 1971): auditing all expenditure from the Consolidated Funds of India and the states, the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts; auditing government companies and corporations; conducting compliance (legality), financial and performance audits (economy, efficiency and effectiveness) and propriety audits; and submitting audit reports to the President (for the Union) and Governors (for states), which are laid before legislatures and examined by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The CAG acts as a 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the PAC. Notable reports include those on the 2G spectrum allocation (2010), Commonwealth Games (2011) and coal block allocation (2012). Limitations: post-facto audit only, no power to punish, and audit of secret service expenditure is limited.
section-154: The Ministry of Finance has five departments: the Department of Economic Affairs (which prepares the Union Budget, manages external finance, currency and coinage and capital markets, and publishes the Economic Survey); the Department of Expenditure (public expenditure management, pay commissions, the Office of the Controller General of Accounts); the Department of Revenue (direct and indirect taxes, through the Central Board of Direct Taxes and Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs; GST Council secretariat); the Department of Financial Services (banks, insurance, pensions); and the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM, disinvestment).

Functions: formulating fiscal policy, preparing and implementing the budget, mobilising resources through taxation and borrowing, controlling public expenditure, managing public debt, coordinating with the Reserve Bank of India on monetary and financial matters, administering financial institutions, and representing India in international financial institutions (IMF, World Bank, G20 finance track). The Chief Economic Adviser advises the government. The Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends the sharing of taxes between the Union and states.
section-156: Meaning: public administration is the implementation of public policies through government organisations. Wilson (1887) founded the discipline and proposed the politics-administration dichotomy; White, Gulick, Simon, Waldo and Appleby offered definitions emphasising management, policy implementation and public character. Public and private administration share techniques but differ in purpose, accountability, legal framework and scale.

Scope: POSDCORB view (Gulick) of managerial functions; the subject-matter view (functions of departments such as defence, education, health); integral and managerial views; and modern scope including organisation, personnel, finance, policy, local government, development administration, accountability, governance and e-governance. Evolution: classical theories (Taylor, Fayol, Weber), human relations (Mayo), behavioural approach (Simon), systems and ecological approaches (Fred Riggs), New Public Administration (1968), New Public Management (1980s-1990s) and governance.

Significance: implementation of laws and policies, service delivery, law and order, development and welfare, crisis management, continuity and stability, and nation-building in developing countries. In India, administrative reforms include the Administrative Reforms Commissions (1966, 2005), RTI, citizens' charters, e-governance, direct benefit transfers and Mission Karmayogi. Effective administration is essential for good governance.
section-157: Scientific management (Taylor, 1911): one best way of doing work; time-and-motion studies; scientific selection and training; division of responsibility between management and workers; incentive wages; contributions - efficiency, standardisation and systematic management; criticisms - treats workers as machines, ignores human factors, causes monotony and alienation. Related classical theories include Fayol's 14 principles and Gulick's POSDCORB.

Human relations approach (Mayo, Hawthorne experiments, 1924-1932): workers are social beings; informal groups, morale, communication, participation and supervision influence productivity; the organisation is a social system; non-economic rewards matter. Later behavioural theories (Maslow, McGregor, Herzberg) developed motivation theory. Criticisms: overemphasis on informal relations and human factors, neglect of structure and economic incentives, possible manipulation.
